title: A Crack in the Darkness 𓇳

blocks.text: “The present moment is the only moment available to us, and it is the door to all moments.”
THICH NHẤT HẠNH

The power of soulless inhumanity, which has always been a pervasive albeit masked force in our politics, is now on full display. Not Republican or Democrat, but psychopath. That is the Geist that inhabits now the White House, a love of death, the desire for a brief flash, the momentary vanishing of impotence the moment bombs fall.

We can no longer pretend the foundations are intact. Arms contracts and political debts are the forces that guide. The system requires endless war while healthcare, education, and feeding the poor have become preposterous propositions. More insane still: the religious fantasy on all sides, covenants that seem to prefer apocalypse over communication. We hold tight onto the worn-out blanket of these bedtime stories told by our ancestors, who had never imagined electricity, AI, climate change, or universal human rights. All this childish hubris. The chosen. The right. Anything rather than humbly admitting that we all wish to continue breathing.

The shock of what I see today glues my jaw to the floor. I listened well in Sunday School. There seemed to be a refrain when it came to the teachings of Christ: charity, forgiveness, love, and healing. How could any interpretation of love ever be more farcical than that which we see now masquerading in American flags?

It’s enough insanity to make a person want to say that everything is lost. And yet, how can we live, how can we resist? In the face of such a pernicious, illogical, and all-consuming beast, what tactics are most adaptive? Firstly, we must not rest complicit in our silence bought cheaply with comfort: endless sports spectacles or season twelve of another meaningless show, likes on socials for doing socially safe things while we scroll in climate-controlled rooms. What are all these worth when our minds reel and our hearts seethe with the injustice that we desperately try to ignore and avoid? Anesthetized in stimulation, until we don’t even respond when the missiles finally start to fly over our own heads. Resistance is medicine in a sick world.

And yet, secondly, we cannot out of guilt or crisis self-impose a cessation in the celebration of this miracle called life. Like Toi Derricotte said, “joy is resistance”. Each breath sings it, even if the mind feels hopelessly depressed as it muddles through media. In the face of ever-fresh hypocrisy and abomination, all of nature is buzzing with a desire for life. Nature dares even to mock the sadomasochistic human machine by singing its fecundity and ecstasy in every sunset and sunrise. Homeostasis, harmony, is spontaneously sought in every cell of every manifestation we call life. Because in truth, life loves life. Death might be necessary, might be revolutionary for evolutionary forces to perform, but worshiping death would be a deep misreading of the whole story. Like worshiping the last page of a chapter but not reading the ones that lead you there. Only a decapitated ego worships death. And yet this motherless child, who has forgotten he depends on the earth for life, works around the clock in Washington, in Tel Aviv, in Tehran worshipping the death of the “other” without recognizing he is inevitably conjuring his own destruction.

We must maintain our desire simultaneously to resist and to live well. Quiet comfort and existential regret are both tactics of the oppressor to win the war of soul capture. Numb you with entertainment or collapse you with guilt; either way you are removed from the field. First, you must recognize that the war is not only being waged out there but most fundamentally in you. But will you cave to its commands? Or will you carry on the work to celebrate this miracle called life? Even in the midst of the Holocaust, Viktor Frankl recounts: “Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one’s own way. And there were always choices to make. Every day, every hour, offered the opportunity to make a decision, a decision which determined whether you would or would not submit to those powers which threatened to rob you of your very self, your inner freedom.”
—Man’s Search for Meaning (1946)

I believe we must maintain our effort to be in the world, and all the while to transcend it. Wise we would be to know our transcendental side. There is something in you, reading this now, that remains eternally unperturbed by the chaos and explosions around. There is a light that burns true in all this religious fanaticism. But the revelation is it doesn’t belong to any particular people, or nation, or tribe — it is the brilliance we are so completely blinded by we can only give cheap descriptions like ‘Life’.  We would do well to shore up our soul in that deep harbor. Lest we might lose ourselves in the same frenzy and fear as those who have obtained everything but have lost the Essential, and chronically feel the mania of never enough. Cleave to the light, for it is that which now is even illuminating the darkness we find.

Thomas Merton, the great Christian mystic, stated it plainly enough, that we must know peace to sow peace: “The rush and pressure of modern life are a form, perhaps the most common form, of… innate violence. To allow oneself to be carried away by a multitude of conflicting concerns, to surrender to too many demands, to commit oneself to too many projects, to want to help everyone in everything, is to succumb to violence. The frenzy of our activism neutralizes our work for peace. It destroys our own inner capacity for peace. It destroys the fruitfulness of our own work, because it kills the root of inner wisdom which makes work fruitful.” — Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander (1966)

Our practice must include getting to know the aspect within us that isn’t up against the test of time, soaking in it like a warm bath every chance we get; and yet in the same breath we must meet the challenge that this darkening human dream asks of us now. There is no escape from this great archetypal battle, whether we want it or not; all of us are being called on, our balance is being tested. All of us are being asked by the great force of life: When it comes to love and nourishing life, will you do what, in your heart, you know to be right?
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते॥
yoga-sthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṁ tyaktvā dhanañjaya |
siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṁ yoga uchyate ||
“Perform your duty established in yoga, abandoning attachment, O Arjuna, being indifferent to success and failure. This equanimity is called yoga.”
— Bhagavad Gītā 2.48
Tantralokā III.130
Devanāgarī
इत्थं प्रकाशातत्त्वस्य सोमसूर्याग्निताऽस्थितिः ।
अपि मुख्यम् तत्प्रकाशामात्रवत्त्वं न व्यपोह्यते ॥१३०॥
IAST
itthaṃ prakāśa-tattvasya soma-sūrya-agnitā sthitiḥ |
api mukhyam tat-prakāśa-mātratvaṃ na vyapohyate || 130 ||
Meaning
Consciousness appears as soma (nectar, soothing), sūrya (illumination), and agni (intensity, fire).
And yet its true nature as pure light (prakāśa-mātra) is never lost.

There is a verse I came across in the Tantralokā yesterday, and it struck me with its metaphorical depth and potency. It speaks of the three primary forms of light the ancients knew and that illuminated their lives: soma, sūrya, agni — moon, sun, and fire.

Its easy to muse on these wondrous lights: the rays of sun that catch heavy eyelids early in the morning; the billowing glow of a full autumn moon; the single candle at the center of an altar, bringing golden visages and deities to life. By these lights are revealed ten thousand textures and countless hues. Yet when all those varieties seem to speak of difference and divison, we must recall their singular essence. Like following the rays of color back through a prism, we find their source; one shade remains: pure light. This is the essential tantric insight.

We experience infinite varieties of consciousness - for every hue of color we can name, so too a mood: sweet sadness, mindless joy, mirthful anger, a spirited depression. These verbal designations fall infinitely short of consciousness’s true capacity. Yes, we can say “sweet sadness,” and maybe have some shared notion, but what is occurring now is this never-before-seen moment: the yellow of a leaf, the bark of a tree, a distant sound - the breaking of a twig, a wind that is cool but not unsettling.

To speak is to gesture toward experience, but speech alone can never match its infinite texture. In fact our linguistic and mental observations themselves are just another layer of texture, spices adding flavor, contributing to the never before tasted rasa of this moment. The wonder is how all these infinitely unique experiences are composed of one essence, the miracle of the one playing as the many.
The variegated mind reveals its innate qualities in phases, in lights:
the moon: the soothing calm after a hard day;
the sun: the clarity of knowing exactly what must be done;
the fire: the pulsing focus of emails, lunch, workouts, relations, difficult conversations.

And yet all these experience occur in the same eye, like these three lights harken back to the single source. In spiritual practice, these lights illuminate different steps on the path, different stages of the breath.
Moon — The Exhale, The Soothing Light

There is that moment of cool, nourishing calm when the weight of embodiment and responsibility begins to fall off. Through the meditative impulse to let go, we loosen the grip on everything that held us, tied as it were to the whipping post of our own ego’s expectations.

In that brief reprieve from the engineered obsession to do and be more, we may taste the nectar of simply being at peace with our own minds. This moon-light, this cooling softness, can be felt as the exhale, the easing out of effort and stress.
Sun — The Inhale, The Light of Realization

Then there is the sun: the realization that startles, rearranges, clarifies. When it rises, the shapes that once frightened us in the night reveal themselves in their true form. What we thought was a menacing figure, death over our shoulder, turns out to be a blossoming tree, a nourisher and protector grounding and guiding this life-force eternal.

This solar clarity allows us to see ourselves and our circumstances for what they are: a miracle. It shows us where we want to go and how to get there. And so we can associate this sunlight of understanding with the inhale — taking in the gift of a new breath, a new moment, a new day, a new life, full of wonder and possibility.
Fire — The Kumbhaka, The Transforming Flame

And finally, fire: the transformative flame. Sacred fire, stolen from the gods not only to guide the eyes but to transform whatever it touches. Fire brings out the essence of things, burns away impurities, and keeps alive the dream of warmth in all seasons.

In spiritual practice, this fire is indispensable, arising both by effort and grace. We may have inspiring insights and profound sighs of relief, but it is fire that harmonizes these forces and manifests them as our personified being. We sit in our own inner fire - the heat of austerity and devotion, the longing for merging, ecsatcy, and peace. Through the courage to stay in the flame, we alloy ourselves into something of richer caliber, while our confusions and collapses into ignorance naturally melt away.
This fire corresponds to the pause, the kumbhaka, the sitting down in the center, the abundant emptiness that transforms.
One Light, One Breath
And yet the teaching insists: all of these lights are truly one, prakāśa-mātra, pure light.
Just as all phases of the breath compose one breath, so too do the various lights of spiritual life compose one single process: awakening to the all-pervading, all-consuming radiance.
When we understand that every shade of experience expresses the universal Light, then we can allow ourselves to be illumined at every moment, regardless of emotional tone or energetic hue.
This is the never-ending story of self-realization:
the recognition that even your bones are made of nothing but Light.

title: While the devil is in the details, the divine is in the principle 𓇳

blocks.text: I write this at 2 a.m., unable to clear my mind of the cloudy impressions of an apparently darker time. Perhaps, as someone who has lived outside of the U.S. for a long time, I’m not qualified to write on domestic topics—maybe my finger is further from the pulse. Perhaps, given my profession as a yoga instructor, I might seem unqualified to espouse political philosophy and political science. Yet perhaps it is this distance that better allows me to see shapes on the horizon, like icebergs threatening imminent danger. As a student of yoga and psychology, I am familiar with the human mind’s ability to mislead itself, with the ego’s tendency to concretize illusions at every step, providing a sense of justification, security, and superiority. Perhaps a yogi is imagined as someone beyond the purview of preference and politics. But when it comes to an opportunity to help manifest wisdom and compassion, a person who claims to have character cannot ignore the invitation to act. This election, appearing monumental and posing questions of human goodnes, gives me the impetus to challenge the ways in which we might be seeing our situation.

Cognitive dissonance is one of the first concepts students learn in psychology. It’s the tension we experience when our beliefs, values, and actions don’t align, which eventually results in changing one of them to feel whole again. Think back to 2001: how many people truly believed the Iraqi government was involved in September 11th? But somehow the vast majority of voters and elected officials could do the cognitive gymnastics to equate any Middle Eastern Muslims to enemies. A persistent belief in fantastically destructive weapons was used as justification, until the awkward truth finally had to be shown, none could be found.

Today, cognitive dissonance might explain why we value some human lives more than others. This is perhaps the factor that lets us feel Israeli suffering is more real than Palestinian suffering, the factor that helps us believe a war in Europe is more tragic than a war in Sudan, the factor that enables us to see a migrant worker as less human than an American citizen. Through the mental gymnastics of seeing suffering but not speaking or acting against it, we solidify the illusion that someone is more worthy of goodness and life than somebody else. We are now living in this mass hallucination where some human lives are valued more than others; and until we collectively break out of this illusion, we will never truly be at peace.

And how is this week’s election any different? We are comfortably lining up to vote with our cognitive dissonance glasses on, unable to perceive the shades of cruelty, narcissism, incompetence, and malevolence right before our very eyes. And yet, if you don’t realize you are wearing these glasses, you might ask where any of these elements can be found. But would you be willing to take a step back from your deeply held views? Would you be willing to see an underlying unity amidst the diversity?

The realities we hide from when lost in our dissonance are as follows: threats of jailing political opponents (imagine being sent to jail for a piece like this), promises to deport millions of people who want to experience the same well-being that we all do (inevitably separating families and wreaking havoc on multinational stability), the clear and willful maneuvers to subvert the results of a presidential election (for the first time in American history), evidence of drives towards concentrated and total power, lack of concern about conflicts of interest (having elected leaders and their cronies making massive financial gains from public power), giving control of one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals to someone who has shown themselves to be capricious and incompetent, giving control of the world’s largest economy to someone who is a climate change denier, along with a staggering list of racist, sexist, and other xenophobic claims. Because these facts are so inherently insidious, we find more and more fantastic justifications, as if by magic, to shield our eyes from them. This threat of an American demagogue is not one we can take lightly.

Demagoguery is no new phenomenon. From Caesar’s consolidation of Rome’s republic and coronation as dictator (his official title) to Nero’s voracious and vicious vanity, from Hitler’s to Stalin’s scapegoating of millions of people in their ideological brutality. Haven’t we seen this type of rhetoric and thinking repeat too often? It’s the same rhetoric that was being laughed at and cheered for last week in Madison Square Garden last week. Will we laugh and cheer if we become the cosigners of moral devastation and mass human suffering?

The French philosopher René Girard pointed out the persistent and pernicious human tendency to scapegoat. His work on mimetic theory suggests that human groups find unity by identifying a so-called “out-group” to blame for collective social and moral ills. Girard suggests that while this process might be initially unifying, it leads to cycles of violence and suffering. Perhaps we think we are too advanced and too rational to be caught by the same psychological forces. But this pride might be disastrous. Is that a risk worth taking? How many generations regret the suffering brought by their own delusional cycles of scapegoating? What would they implore us to see, to do today? Is it not clear that the same elements are coalescing now that led to tragedy prior? Alongside scapegoating, there is the consolidation of power, erosion of opposition, and the discrediting of vital institutions and scientific knowledge. Can you also appreciate these shapes on the horizon?

Reading this, dear friend, you might say, while I am aware of all those threats, I have good reason to neglect or disbelieve them. Perhaps you think: my vote is simply guided by potential personal gain, or as an act of rebellion against a system that props up one puppet politician after another, or the belief that all this talk is unnecessarily alarmist, or that I can’t agree with the details of her policies. Finally, you might say my vote is a necessary evil to attain a virtuous end. But where is the virtue in a world where you have a bigger slice of a rotting pie? With mass deportation, we’re discussing dissolving the vital roles played by millions of individuals. Will you pick the fruit in the fields? Will you quit your air-conditioned office job to build houses in the Arizona sun? Will you leave work early to care of your kid when there is a sudden shortage of childcare? And this doesn’t yet factor the human experience of so many individuals and families who we see so scapegoated at rally after rally.

You might not think Kamala Harris is qualified, you may think she is thrust undemocratically upon you, you might think the details of her platform are sparse. But while the devil is in the details, the divine is in the principle. This is a choice between a vision of unity versus one of division. If I may even wax emotional, it is a decision between love and fear, between kindness and hate. I am supporting Kamala Harris because it is a clear and obvious choice of someone who is earnestly speaking of unity. We as the people must drive her to that collective good, but unlike her alternative, she is someone who is not beyond reproach. Compare that to someone who is cynically beyond all criticism, who treats truth and the government like his plaything. The choice is abundantly clear.

In an ideal sense, government plays the role of protecting and fostering the growth of its people. But we, as people, must be wise enough to see beyond borders and passports to recognize that all people want the same things we do: health, happiness, and security. These are natural principles, genetically embedded and expressed by all conscious beings. When we honor these needs in others, we’re not just upholding their well-being; we’re reinforcing our own. True wisdom lies in shedding the illusion of separateness and recognizing that if we wish something for ourselves, we must support it for all.

In Buddhist teachings, this is called the realization of "emptiness" (śūnyatā), the understanding that all beings are interconnected, all of us are made of everything else. We’ve heard the myth of the self-made man for so long that our cognitive dissonance makes this teaching difficult to realize. But we can dissolve the painful illusion of a separate self by meditating on the truth that every breath we take, every sip of water we drink, every morsel of food we eat, even the language we think in, was not made by us. We are all the fluid manifestation of the same source, the vast universe of causes and conditions. We can also call this emptiness oneness. Sūnyatā-karuṇā-garbha: Oneness is the womb of compassion. From the view of interconnectedness, compassion (karuṇā) naturally arises, as one cannot truly harm others without ultimately harming oneself. Look at the truth of this operating in historical examples of cruelty that one group has inflicted upon another. Isn’t it the case that inevitably both groups suffer as one? If we’re brave enough to look at the survivors of war, we would see that the victors continue to suffer the pain of the vanquished. Emptiness shows us that we cannot escape the global environment that we collectively create. So now the question is: which kind of world do we want to live in?

This vision of emptiness isn’t simply some Buddhist nonsense; it’s clearly echoed in the teaching of Jesus. In John 13:34, he says, "A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another." How could we aspire to emulate that great teacher, if we are imbibing in venomous theories about people who don’t look like us or speak the same language as us? These words are here to break us out of the illusion that self and other are different, promoting acts that enshrine love rather than fear. Your vote is that act. How is it the case that a self-proclaimed Christian in America today is more likely to vote for someone who has such a disgraceful record of bigotry and misogyny? So, dear friend, if you vote, remember: this election is a referendum on our theory of life and humanity. The question is love or fear. And if you are not participating in this election, we are all still equally called, in our great acts and small, to create the world we want to experience by offering it to all.

title: Free Will and Cosmic Consciousness: Our Place in the Universe𓅊

blocks.text:
"By intense awareness and union with the pure essence of reality, one is freed from the limited individual powers."
 Śuddha-tattva-sandhānād vā apaśuśaktiḥ
 शुद्धतत्त्वसन्धानाद्वापशुशक्तिः
 (Śiva Sūtra 1.16)
vā = or
śuddha-tattva = the Pure Principle i.e. the Highest Śiva
sandhānād = by constant awareness
apaśuśaktiḥ = becomes like one in whom the binding power existing in the limited self is absent.
1. Are we Truly Free?

An ancient question continues to perplex philosophers, scientists, and spiritual seekers today: Do we really choose, are we truly free to decide, or are we merely acting out the script of some universal playwright, or our biology and the randomness of circumstance?  The idea that free will is an illusion is rooted in some of the most refined spiritual philosophies and is also aligned with a plethora of contemporary neuroscientific work. On the surface, this idea might seem quite menacing, almost nihilistic, that nothing I or others do is under our control and therefore we can harm and exploit without ever needing to assign responsibility. But what if, this realization, rather than a cause of despair, was a means for liberation? What if by realizing the deeply interpenetrating nature of all things, from neurons to cosmic consciousness, of essential oneness, served as the fundamental ground to live in greater harmony, compassion, and acceptance?

Recently I listened to Sam Harris interview Robert Sapolsky on his Making Sense podcast, and at first I was taken aback by their view that free will is an utter illusion. But it steadily dawned on me that this view acts as liberative understanding, rather than a constricting one. I will try my best to elucidate that point in a way that also serves to liberate you from an unnecessary and effectively illogical sense of shame.

In this exploration, we will plunge into perspectives of contemporary neuroscience, ancient wisdom from the Śiva Sūtra, and why the realization that we are not the sole authors of our lives is actually an invitation to live more blissfully.
2. Modern Debate Highlights the Ancient Illusion

Neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky and neuroscientist turned philosopher Sam Harris have both coherently argued the position that free will is an utter illusion. And this illusion can be seen through on both biologically and philosophical grounds. According to these writers, our thoughts and actions are shaped by innumerable forces outside of our control, each in turn shaped by other innumerable prior causes. For example, you didn’t choose the religion of your parents, the country you were born in, your sex, the color of your hair or eyes, the socioeconomic backdrop of your upbrining and the neurobiological propensity for the multiplicity of traits you experience as ‘me’ - like what food tastes best to you, how introverted or extroverted you feel, how many hours of sleep is optimal, etc. When we look at the sheer infinity of causes, which influence each other in incalculable ways, there is absolutely no place for an independent ‘self’ to exist who is free to choose. Buddhism 101 anyone?

Imagine a ripple in a pond. It has a certain shape and speed, we could call this its character. Now the ripple doesn’t decide it’s character; rather it’s caused by a stone dropped into the water. Similarly, our selves and behaviors are ripples interacting in a cosmic pond of causality. Each neuron firing, each thought we have, is the result of previous causes, all beyond our personal control, all linked to the infinity of action which has come before. We may feel as though agency, but this is a byproduct of the intricate web of causes and effects. Harris uses the metaphor of wetness and a water molecule. A water molecule in and of itself doesn’t have the property of wetness, rather wetness is an emergent property of millions of water molecules coalescing. So to does a single neuron not contain agency, it simply fires or doesn’t, but across billions of neurons coalescing the feeling of being free to choose emerges, but can this ghost actually be found in the machine?

Modern research suggests most clearly, no. Benjamin Libet’s 1983 experiment still serves as the standard today. Libet found that the brain prepares for an action before we're even aware of deciding to move, suggesting that our sense of conscious control may follow our brain’s decisions rather than leading them. John-Dylan Haynes followed up on Libet’s work in 2008 by using fMRI technology. He demonstrated that scientists could predict participants' choices up to seven seconds before they consciously made the decision, showing that unconscious brain activity precedes conscious decision-making by a significant margin. Further work went on to show that the brain perhaps demonstrates some ability to veto one of these ‘unconscious’ decisions, perhaps offering some form of “free-wont”.  But in Harris’s and Sapolsky’s view that entire veto process would also be based on the inescapable influence of our unchosen psychobiology and lived experience. Due to these reasonings and findings many neuroscientists now hold that our sense of making conscious decisions is just an illusion.
3. Our Intuitions and Counterarguments

There is, of course, a debate from other formidable thinkers on this point. Take Daniel Dennet for example, he suggests a contemporary form of compatibilism, where both free will and determinism exist simultaneously. He reasons in his work Freedom Evolves (2003), as most of us our likely to do, that we can still consider ourselves to be “free” if through rational deliberation and reflection we can align our actions with our deeply held desires and intentions. At first glance, we like this seemingly more nuanced approach, as it serves as the basis for our entire human sphere full of moral agency and possibility. It allows us to justify both reward and punishment to persons who we consider the author of their good and bad acts. Taken to its furthest extent this is the philosophy of the saved and the damned, those who deserve suffering or happiness because of their free choices.

Yet this view has deep logical inconsistencies. Aligning our actions to our desires and intentions might be more coherent, perhaps even resulting in happiness, but those desires and intentions are not our own. Every desire we have today is shaped by biological or social forces, I might desire a wonderful life, however I define it, but certainly that definition is based on biological and psychological needs which are clearly outside of my choosing. If we are brave enough to stretch our minds to the point, we can touch the truth that all of this was beyond any personal choosing. And rather than being depressing, this is a cause for liberation.
4. True Freedom and Where to Find It

Perhaps today’s materialist science leaves us with a cold stark feeling of determinism. But centuries prior texts like the Śiva Sūtra explored the nature of reality and the self, showing that while an individual being or jīva, is bound by cirumstance, the true self remains absolutely free.
In Śiva Sūtra 1.16, we find this profound teaching:

Śuddha-tattva-sandhānād vā apaśuśaktiḥ
 शुद्धतत्त्वसन्धानाद्वापशुशक्तिः
 "Or by constant awareness of the Pure Priniciple, he becomes like one in whom the binding power existing in the limited self is absent." -Trans. Jaideva Singh

The verse points to the illusion of individuality: our sense of being separate entities, literally here as animals or paśu, with our own sense of power, śakti. In the non-dual Śiva Tantra freedom belongs not to the apparent individual but to the Universal Consciousness itself. It is this śuddha-tattva, the Pure Principle, that is both the original cause and the all-pervasive substance. It is both the rock thrown in the water and the interacting dance of ripples. When we recognize the śuddha-tattva as everything we observe, from our cells to the sunset, we transcend then illusion of being a self-determined and individual being, and realize ourselves to be what we truly are: the comic essence itself.

Just as modern science shows that our decisions are shaped by biological process, so to do the Śiva Sūtras that all our thoughts and actions are the direct expressions of universal consciousness. There is no room for real separate agents, only one unified essence, experiencing itself in and through its infinite modifications.

In fact, the highest principle in this non-dual Śiva Tantra is free-will, or svātantrya. This is not the free-will of some limited or contracted ‘I’, rather this is the cosmic freedom that is the force that put the infinitude of causes in motion, that is the cause that led you to be reading these very words right now. We attain true freedom not through by determining our desires and decisions, but by realizing that we are identical to the force that determined and desired all of this.  At the absolute level, we are one with the free, creative consciousness that is the source of all.
5. Liberation from Guilt and Blame

At first, the idea that we don’t have free will may feel unsettling. If we aren’t in control, then what’s the point? Why bother trying to be good or striving to achieve anything? The answer lies in a profound shift in perspective—one that is the dawning of an authentic spiritual life.

Freedom from Guilt and Shame: If our thoughts and actions are determined by forces beyond our control, we can begin to let go of the heavy burden of guilt, shame, and inadequacy. No longer do we need to judge ourselves harshly for not being “good enough” or making mistakes. We are simply expressions of the universe, unfolding according to its laws. The teaching of apaśuśaktiḥ (freedom from limited powers) encourages us to throw off the burden of constant self-condemnation.

Self-Acceptance: Contemporary philosophy and the Śiva Sūtras teach us that there is nothing inherently flawed about what we do and how we think. Every success, every failure, every idiosyncrasy is an expression of the infinite web of causes and effects. This is Indra’s Net, we live in a holographic universe where everything contains traces of everything else. Nothing is independent of anything else. We are perfect manifestations of Nature or the pure essence of reality. Recognizing this frees us from the toxic need for perfectionism.

Compassion for Others: Understanding that others, too, are the product of circumstances beyond their control fosters deeper compassion. When someone acts out of anger, fear, or confusion, we can recognize that they are not choosing those actions in a vacuum—they are expressions of a vast network of causes. Just as we seek to be understood, we can extend that same understanding to others, breaking down the walls of judgment.
6. Moving with Nature Instead of Against It

Accepting that the ego has not real freedom is freedom, freedom from the illusion of control. Life is not something we need to battle or control, but something we can flow with. Like the ripple in the pond, we are the motion of the universe. The Śiva Sūtra reminds us that when we recall our pure essence, śuddha tattva, we transcend the illusion of separateness and realize that we are part of the cosmic dance.

In a practical sense, this means letting go of the constant need to "fix" ourselves, others, and the world around us. We can still strive for positive change, that is of course natural intelligence, in fact it is Nature’s Intelligence, moving though us in every cell of our being. Great peace can be felt and wisdom implemented in trusting the intelligence moving through us rather than making it a limited personal possession to be proud or ashamed of.
7. Practical Implementation: How to Live with This Understanding
How might it be helpful to apply this refined position of freedom to our lives? Here are a few possibilities:

Let Go of Perfectionism: Realizing that you are not the sole author of your actions releases the pressure to always get things right. You are already and always enough as you are—a pure expression of Nature or Śuddha Tattva.

Cultivate Compassion: When you understand that everyone, including yourself, is a product of causes beyond control, you naturally develop more empathy for yourself and others. You are free to forgive more easily and hold less resentment. We can advocate for systems of justice that champion rehabilitation and restraint rather than punishment and harm.

Celebrate Your Place in the Universe: Rather than feeling like a small, isolated being, reframe your existence as a wave in the ocean or a jewel in Indra’s Net. Every thought, action, and experience is part of a great interconnected process, you reflect everything else, and everything else reflects you. See the beauty that you are the universal expressed in dynamic, infinite uniqueness.
8. Conclusion: The Beauty of Being a Cosmic Manifestation

In both the scientific and spiritual logic, we find a profound message: we are not isolated beings, struggling for control in a chaotic world. Instead, we are part of a larger, interconnected flow—whether you call it the laws of nature or Śuddha Tattva. This recognition frees us from guilt, blame, and the burden of regret.

For the sanity of our human world we must overcome the invasive intuition that we are somehow flawed or broken; we are immediate manifestations of the universe, ripples in the cosmic water. The realization that we have no free will as assumed in not one of dread, but of beauty—we are all expressions of the one infinite intelligence, and in that, we find our real freedom.

We are fortunate to have great spirtual cartographers who have charted various territories of the inner depths for us. Their work is here to guide us, especially when we feel without direction. A spiritual map ingeniously charted by a modern guru in an ancient tongue is found in Sri Brahmanda Saraswati’s Sanskrit verse. This verse, filled with deep wisdom, guides us on our inner journey: Oṁ bodhi-rūpaṁ bodhi-sattvaṁ bodhi-gamyam anāmayam | parama-satyaṁ parama-śāntaṁ parama-brahma parāt-param||

With a good quality map, it’s much easier to know where we are and where we are going. And all good maps contain clear landmarks that help to orient us when we have lost our way. Maps of the spirtual sort are filled with words rather than images, symbols rather than coordinates; and when these blaze clear for us we can aim ourselves in the direction that we desire to go.

We would be foolish however to think the map is itself the territoriy. Just as a verbal description of the Amazon Rainforest cannot replace the experience of being there, spiritual teachings are guides, not the final experience.

Imagine you recently visited the Amazon. Your description could certainly help me understand what that place is like. But it would be a cheap substitute for the experience of the rainforest itself. Still your description would be valuable for me to hear. You explain it is a place that is teeming with life, full of animals and plants of all kinds, richly moist and fragrant, and drenched in an infinity of shades of green. So that if I find myself on a parched piece of land without any life in sight, I wouldn’t mistakenly assume that I was in the Amazon. I can’t be sure of what the rainforest is like from your map of words, but based on what you shared I can be certain when I’m not there.

This great teacher, Sri Brahmananda, traversed depths and dimensions of being to come back with his depiction of the landscape. Here is a possible rendtion of his verse of the experience of union, of yoga: “It is of the form of awakening, awakening harmony, awakening that is possible to reach, a state that is free from all disease and pain. It is the supreme truth, the supreme peace, the supreme divinity, transcending our conception of the supreme.” It sounds wonderful, but perhaps all these words can’t fully resonate at first glance. Simpiler would be to start with the parts of the map we can relate to.

We can begin with awakening, as it’s the theme of the first half of the verse and an experience we have each day. I am determined to save the president from a group of giant rat people, only to be distracted by a talking sunflower with sunglasses dancing across the sky, reciting poetry to confused clouds while squirrels play jazz in the branches below. And in a flash my eyes open to the morning light coming through the windows. I believed this whole ludicrous fantasy to be real, only to realize I had been dreaming in bed. Great sages, like the Buddha, have said spiritual awakening is just like that.

We take all of this to be real, and then bang. We wake up to a higher reality, a deeper one, and the life we were so lost in is now as ephemeral as last night’s dream. As it would quite confusing to explain the waking world to a dreamer, so too do the sages struggle to convey the reality beyond our five senses. But equipped with a quality map, we can more confidently move in that direction.

Yoga has the form of awakening, it is waking up to a harmony where no flaw or fault can be found. Nothing is missing. And though this awakening to a pure reality might seem terribly obscure from the perspective of this body-mind, he tells us that it is within our reach. That yoga is something we can experience. And we’ll know it because it is a place where pain vanishes. So we know we’re not in the rainforest just yet if sickness and suffering are still the predominant themes of our experience.

The next line challenges us to imagine the highest, parama. The highest truth automatically negates anything that is changing, because it is only temporarily true. If I say to you today is sunny, you might agree, but if we stand outside long enough we can readily see that that truth decays with the passage of time. Even the most brilliant day descends into night. Even the great laws that govern this universe, like gravity, electromagnetism, the strong and weak forces all came into being with time. So even these primordial forces cannot be considered as eternal and supreme truth.

We can see clearly that the yoga Sri Brahmananda refers to is something beyond that which happens within time. And it is considered to be the highest peace, unshakable tranquility. A peace even more profound than a sloth slowly shutting its eyes on a branch where the sun is breaking through the canopy overhead.

This peace is the peace that is the result of sublimation into the divine, yoga. Supreme truth and peace here are equated to God; they are the qualities of the Ultimate Reality. And yet the ultimate is parāt-param, transcending the supreme. Our spiritual guide has included this final caveat for us, first so that we never get stuck on any concept as equaling the supreme itself (of course, as all concepts are inherently dualistic and occur within time), and second, that the magnificence of this mystery is so parodixacal that the transcendental even transcends itself! This is akin to a beautiful Zen koan that breaks open the mind. Perhaps we can frame the perpetual transcending of the transcendant with Kant’s theory of the dynamical sublime in his Critique of Judgment. When we encounter the vastness of nature, it reflects the vastness of our own being, the one eternally conquering the other. Like when your eyes meet the infinitude of the rainforest, it swallows you up whole, and yet somehow it is all contained within your eyes.

In reading all this, we might say, “Wow, I’ve never been to the Amazon, but it sure does sound nice.” And if we really desire to go there, thankfully we have this map and others to know when we are getting closer to that territory. If our days are filled with frusturation, and our nights with insecrutiy, we can know at least that we’re in some desert far away from our desired destination. But when we think, speak, and act in a way that enables us to feel that we’re awakening from a deep slumber, when harmony starts to dawn in our hearts, then perhaps we know we’re on the right track. When we feel the goal of yoga is possible because with practice authenticty and peace blossom in our hearts, perhaps we have started to enter the territory.
Oṁ (ॐ): A sacred sound and spiritual symbol representing the essence of ultimate reality, consciousness, or Atman.
Bodhi (बोधि): Enlightenment or awakening, particularly in a Buddhist context.
Rūpaṁ (रूपम्): Form, shape, or appearance, often contrasted with essence or spirit.
Sattvaṁ (सत्त्वम्): Purity, harmony, and balance, one of the three gunas (qualities) in Indian philosophy.
Gamyam (गम्यम्): Attainable or reachable, often referring to a spiritual goal.
Anāmayam (अनामयम्): Free from disease or pain; a state of health or peace.
Parama (परम): Supreme or highest, often denoting the ultimate or absolute.
Satyaṁ (सत्यम्): Truth or reality, a fundamental principle in Indian philosophy.
Śāntaṁ (शान्तम्): Peaceful, calm, or tranquil, describing inner peace.
Brahma (ब्रह्म): The ultimate reality or cosmic spirit in Hinduism (Brahman), the creator god in the universe (Brahma).
Parāt (परात्): Beyond or supreme, referring to what is transcendent or beyond ordinary perception.

title: From Wave to Ocean𓆡
excerpt: Understanding the Five Afflictions in Patanjali's Yoga Sutra- Avidya, asmita, raga, dvesha, and abhinivesha are the five afflictions in Patanjali’s Yoga Sutra- Avidya is the fundamental ignorance of the real nature of things- Asmita is the attachment to the ego and belief in the 'myth of me'- The practice of vidya involves realizing the eternal nature of the self and resting in the present awareness- Vidya allows one to experience fullness and transcend attachment and resistance

blocks.text: Patanjali's Yoga Sutra 2.3
अविद्यास्मितारागद्वेषाभिनिवेशाः क्लेशाः ॥ २.३ ॥
Avidyā (misapprehension about the real nature of things), asmitā (egoism), rāga (attachment), dveśa (aversion), and abhiniveśa (fear of death) are the five kleśas (afflictions).

Fundamental ignorance is believing that "me" is real, independent from the world, and is the Self. This attachment to body-mind formation is the basis of the 'myth of me', asmita or egotism. Ego thinks it knows. Therefore, it believes it knows what is best to chase and what is best to reject. In doing so, ego operates in a mode that is in opposition to existence, finally feeling that death is the extinguishing of the Self.

We are each like a wave, trying to construct a barrier between ourselves and the ocean, hoping to never be drowned, to never be reabsorbed. Not recognizing the whole time that this wave is the ocean! Thus, we live in insanity, always trying to gather momentum and mass, resisting other waves and the process of time, continually chasing and rejecting in more complicated ways to avoid the inevitable merging back into the Sea, the Source. In running from merging, the wave does not realize that it is resisting its own Self, fulfillment, bliss, freedom, eternality. This is ignorance, thinking that "I am this me here" in opposition to the life that is out there.

Body-mind will always have their waveform. But the wave remains forever the ocean. We will always have our frequencies of color that express, but all those colors never cease to be light. Realizing that is Buddhi, awakening intelligence, which finds light as the basis of all experience, which feels equilibrium in the changing tides. Buddhi contrasts to asmita. And vidya to avidya. Knowing this thinking "me" knows nothing truly, but still being centered in the ineffable light of I AM. Our practice is to orient body-mind to the light like a sunflower following the sun, yet trusting at the same time we are being naturally pulled towards that light (abhyasa/vairagya). Being in the light is vidya, remembering and resting in the ever-present, the now, the light of awareness.

In vidya, we sense the fragrance of fullness, where is there space for the mind to appear that criticizes continually itself and its experience. Ask yourself how can I get attached to or resist something that is always moving, always changing? Have two breaths ever been the same? Getting attached to a snapshot of the river is ignorance. And yet this now, this light, this presence? Isn't it curiously eternal? Where can their be the death of that which is always here? Vidya is finding, resting in and realizing you are that which never dies.

title: Mind the gap…
excerpt: A poetic rendition of a practice prescribed by Sutra 17 of Siva Sutra

blocks.text: Madhyavikāsa मध्यविकास Development of the Middle
A gap between the clouds,
reveals pale blue
limitlessness.
A gap between thoughts,
reveals pure light
awareness.
At the heart of the tumult,
A wheel riding high then low,
is the center from which
radiate
all spokes
Saṃvit (संवित्)
The light which illumines
equally both day and night
Birth and death
Love and hate
Seek to find ground
Upon which all changes play
All players change
And in that light,
Remain
Cage of ribs
heaving from empty to full,
Full to empty again -
pause at the apex
or abyss
And without context
realize the changeless bliss
Bathe in the middle
which contains all opposites
मध्यविकासाच्चिदानन्दलाभः॥१७॥
Madhyavikāsāccidānandalābhaḥ||17||
Siva Sutra
Madhya - middle
Vikāsa - development, unfolding, expansion towards independence
Cit - consciousness, awareness
ānanda - bliss
lābhaḥ - acquisition, realization
From the expansion of the middle, the attainment of consciousness-bliss.

title: Unveiling the Divine Tapestry𓌵
excerpt: This self-weaving tapestry acts as an epic poem, a grand narrative of tumult. It is a story in constant flux, where the threads of the tapestry intertwine into evolution, creating a ceaseless movement of creation and destruction. This self-weaving chimera transcends notions of beautiful and ugly, right and wrong, yet somehow contains all of it – even our human life: struggles, conflicts, and moments of harmony and resolution.

blocks.text: Imagine, if you will, an image—a tapestry which weaves itself. In this tapestry, the weaver, the woven, and the act of weaving are inseparably united, forming a seamless whole. It is a tapestry without boundaries, its patterns extending infinitely in every direction. With each pass of the weaver, the tapestry grows more intricate, as former patterns are expanded upon and new ones take shape. However, amidst this continuous elaboration, certain patterns collide and clash, giving rise to chaos. Yet, out of chaos, a cosmic order emerges, a harmonious synthesis of seemingly disparate elements.

This self-weaving tapestry acts as an epic poem, a grand narrative of tumult. It is a story in constant flux, where the threads of the tapestry intertwine into evolution, creating a ceaseless movement of creation and destruction. This self-weaving chimera transcends notions of beautiful and ugly, right and wrong, yet somehow contains all of it – even our human life: struggles, conflicts, and moments of harmony and resolution. It also echoes the cyclical nature of existence, where patterns repeat and transform, illustrating the interplay between creation and destruction.

The image could go further to suggest that this tapestry exists beyond the confines of space and time. It is not limited by linear progression or the constraints of a fixed narrative. Rather, it is a tapestry of infinite threads, infinite story lines that diverge and converge to shape the universe. The story being written within this tapestry is one that defies conventional notions of beginning, middle, and end. It is a story that is constantly being written, revised, and rewritten, transcending the linear march of time. "The whole is the true; but the whole is nothing other than the essence consummating itself through its development. Of all the moments, only one is the beginning, and this beginning is the actuality of the whole. The beginning is therefore the essence moving itself, and thus it is the self-producing."[1]

This vision of a self-creating, self-knowing, and self-consuming universe resonates with various philosophical schools of interest, particularly the intuition and the inference that the ultimate is beyond the duality of knower and known. The self-creating tapestry as our starting image elucidates the notion of non-duality, where the boundaries between creator and creation dissolve, revealing the interconnectedness of all things. Thus, the tapestry has birthed here the collection of writings called PRAMATA. Theses are the musings and invited discussion concerning this tapestry of Cosmos, which are sourced in our foundational philosophical schools, like Non-dual Shiva Tantra, Hegel’s Dialectical Monism, Spinoza’s Monistic Idealism, Advaita Vedanta, contemporary forms of panpsychism, and the Sufi idea of Wahdat al-wujud.

Now, you might ask, “But what good does it do me to think of the universe as a self-weaving tapestry. What good could it bring to study all these esoteric and metaphysical philosophies?” Its the shifting of perspective that can radically change our life experience. Understanding the universe as a singular self-creating entity and studying non-dual philosophy can have profound implications for how we perceive ourselves and how we engage with the world.

By recognizing that our essence is not confined to the limitations of our individual personalities and bodies, we can transcend the narrow confines of the exhausting ego-drama. This perspective offers liberation from the constant anxieties of our individual and alienated life, allowing us to embrace a broader sense of identity and interconnectedness. We can cultivate a deep sense of belonging to the unfolding cosmos, understanding that we are part of, and more importantly we are, a larger story that transcends time and space. As Rumi is often quoted, “Do not feel lonely, the entire universe is inside you. Stop acting so small. You are the universe in ecstatic motion.”[2]

If we perceive ourselves as an expression of the universe, continuously unraveling and reweaving, the fear of annihilation dissipates. We realize that our essence is not confined to this particular lifetime. We give up the vampires in our minds of total annihilation, or a redundant afterlife of any various heaven or hell, where we still are subsumed by memory, longing, and neurosis. This recognition of deathlessness, or amṛta in Sanskrit, empowers us to live fearlessly, embracing the creative impulse within us and expressing it authentically.

Moreover, this perspective invites us to rest in the inherent intelligence and harmony of the universe. We can let go of the need to control every aspect of our lives and trust in the natural flow of existence. It could allow us to find deeper peace and acceptance, knowing that everything is unfolding exactly as it should, guided by the innate intelligence of the weaver-woven-weaving (we can see why the term God becomes convenient over time).

Finally, this understanding also brings a profound shift in our relationship with mortality, naturally a feeling of interconnectedness encourages us to engage with others in a spirit of compassion, generosity, and unity. We recognize that the energy we share with others is ultimately the energy of the universe itself. By offering our insights, time, and energy, we contribute to the beautification of the tapestry where we are, here and now, enriching the lives of those around us and our own, fostering a collective sense of interconnectedness and well-being. Furthermore, interconnectedness ignites a circle of compassion to see that suffering is shared by all. We could sense a mutually responsibility for this here-now, this loka, that we are weaving as the universe in ecstatic motion. We could gravitate more easily towards non-violence, as we have an arguably innate preference for beautiful and peaceful patterns. And most importantly, a respect for all life would more easily emerge, one that recognizes the inherent dignity of all beings and things, as infinitely equal (and yet infinitely unique!) expressions of the whole.

In this way, viewing the universe as a self-weaving tapestry and exploring esoteric and metaphysical philosophies can profoundly transform our experience of life. It invites us to embrace our true nature, express our creativity, find peace in the unfolding of existence, and cultivate compassion and unity with others. Ultimately, it offers a framework for living a life of purpose, meaning, and interconnectedness.
Sources
[1] Hegel, "Science of Logic," Book I, §178
[2] Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī., & Barks, C. (1996). The essential Rumi. 1st HarperCollins paperback ed. San Francisco, CA, Harper.
